title: The literal meanings of city names

entries.note: From an old Slavic word meaning swamp; the land is still so swampy that building sites must be drained with pipes.
A Slavic language still spoken by a few people in Brandenburg around Berlin, explaining why [[see:Berlin]] has a Slavic name.
Compared with [[see:Berlin]] as another city built on a swamp.
German place-name ending that corresponds to English [[same-root:-thorpe]].
English place-name ending, the equivalent of German [[same-root:-dorf]].
German place-name ending, as in [[see:Hamburg]], the same as English [[same-root:-bury]] or [[same-root:-borough]].
English place-name ending equivalent to German [[same-root:-berg]].
English place-name ending equivalent to German [[same-root:-berg]].
On a map translating German place names into English equivalents, it becomes Hambury.
Translated into an English equivalent it becomes Frankford, since the -furt corresponds to ford.
Means a stud yard for horses, so its English equivalent would be Studgard.
Its English equivalent on the translated map is Manheim.
English and German forms developed separately from Old High German Munichen; both mean the place of the monks, related to [[same-root:monk]] and [[same-root:minchen]].
An old English word meaning something like an abbey, used for [[see:Munich]] on the translated map.
Comedian whose surname resembles [[see:minchen]], the English rendering of Munich.
Related to [[same-root:Munich]]; basically means solitary one, related to the prefix [[same-root:mono-]], a Mediterranean origin as with many Christian words.
Another monk-related place name, meaning the same as English [[same-root:minster]].
English word given as the equivalent of [[same-root:Münster]].
Prefix related to [[same-root:monk]], not Germanic in origin.
Myth says it is named after [[see:Romulus]], but probably the reverse; other theories link it to a root meaning to flow, strength or hill city, or Etruscan.
Mythical founder of [[see:Rome]], twin of [[see:Remus]], raised by a she-wolf; his name was more likely derived from Rome than vice versa.
Twin of [[see:Romulus]], killed by him after a dispute over the location of Rome.
River that one theory says the name [[see:Rome]] refers to, via a root meaning to flow.
Formerly the Czech Republic; its founding myth claims it is named after the brother [[see:Czech]], though the men are named after the countries.
One of three mythical brothers with [[see:Lech]] and [[see:Rus]]; he founded Czechia, but was named after the country.
Mythical brother who founded Poland, named after the country rather than vice versa; also a famous Polish beer.
Mythical brother who founded Russia, named after the country rather than vice versa.
Named after the Romans, who are named after [[see:Rome]], possibly named after [[see:Romulus]]: a little Roman nesting doll.
From a plural of an unknown pre-Greek word; once singular, it became plural as merged settlements; [[gave:Athena]] her name, not vice versa.
Goddess named after [[from:Athens]], since the ending appears in place names; she won the city by giving the first domesticated olive tree, beating [[see:Poseidon]].
Hypothesised language behind about a thousand unexplained Greek words, including the source of [[see:Athens]].
Another plural Greek place name, like [[see:Athens]], from a collection of merged settlements.
Competed with [[see:Athena]] for Athens by striking a saltwater spring with his trident, which the citizens couldn't drink.
King who judged the gifts of [[see:Athena]] and [[see:Poseidon]] in the founding myth of Athens.
Means victory in Greek; Rob wonders whether the word or the goddess of victory came first.
Once thought to mean threshold, then forward or rapid, after a Vltava crossing; recently linked to Old Czech [[from?:praziti]], to burn.
Nickname for [[see:Prague]] from a count by [[see:Bernard Bolzano]]; today about 500 are estimated.
19th-century mathematician whose count gave Prague the nickname [[see:city of 100 spires]].
Throwing out of a window; Jess says we have the word because so many people were thrown from windows in Prague.
Three events; the first was named only after the second, later demoted to the one-and-a-half defenestration because an official one needs killings and war.
Slavic possessive suffix (-ov, -ev, -iv) meaning belonging to, or place of, as in [[see:Kiev]] and [[see:Plovdiv]].
Means belonging to the stick, with the possessive [[see:-ov]] suffix; nobody knows why.
Bulgarian city meaning belonging to Philip, invoking its Greek name [[from:Philippopolis]].
Greek name for the place that became [[gave:Plovdiv]], meaning Philip's town.
Another Slavic possessive place-name ending (-ska, -isk), as in [[see:Minsk]].
Capital of Belarus, meaning belonging to the river Menka, with the [[see:-sk]] suffix.
Feminine form of [[see:-sk]], used before a feminine noun such as square in the name of a square.
Slavic element meaning town, as in [[see:Leningrad]] and [[see:Stalingrad]]; [[same-root:gorod]] is another rendering of it.
Former name of St Petersburg, an example of [[see:-grad]].
Now known as Volgograd; an example of [[see:-grad]].
Another rendering of [[same-root:-grad]], meaning town, as in [[see:Nizhny Novgorod]].
Nizhny means low, nov means new (like [[same-root:novel]]) and [[see:gorod]] means town: low new town.
Compared with the nov meaning new in [[see:Nizhny Novgorod]].
Means dam in Dutch city names, reflecting the low-lying Netherlands, usually after a river name, as in [[see:Amsterdam]], [[see:Rotterdam]] and [[see:Edam]].
Named after the river [[from:Amstel]] plus [[see:-dam]].
River, and the beer named after it, from a word for current plus a word like German [[same-root:Stelle]], place: water place.
A [[see:-dam]] city on the river Rotte.
A [[see:-dam]] town on the river Ee that gives its name to the cheese; Rob jokes it is the town that is made backwards.
English uses a French name; Dutch Den Haag means the hedge, short for [[from:'s-Gravenhage]], so in English it would be the Haw.
Old name of [[gave:The Hague]], referring to the hedge round the count's hunting grounds.
Title, close to count, behind the graven in [[see:'s-Gravenhage]]; Rob says English lacks it.
Havn is related to [[same-root:haven]] and [[same-root:harbor]]; køben means shop or merchant, related to [[same-root:cheap]] and [[same-root:Chapman]].
Cognate of the havn in [[see:Copenhagen]], once meaning a port or harbour.
Related to the havn in [[see:Copenhagen]].
Related to the copen in [[see:Copenhagen]], meaning shop or merchant.
Name related to the copen in [[see:Copenhagen]], meaning shop or merchant.
Holm means island, though the city spans many islands; stock may mean log, for its timber, or bay.
Os may be Old Norse for estuary; the old explanation, estuary of the [[see:River Lo]], fails because that river doesn't exist, so it's a mystery.
Nonexistent river first recorded in an explanation of [[see:Oslo]], apparently invented to fit that etymology.
Founded after the 1886 gold discovery on the [[see:Witwatersrand]]; unclear which Johan it honours: [[see:Johan Rissik]], [[see:Johan Joubert]], [[see:Johan Meyer]] or [[see:Paul Kruger]].
Long ridge of gold-bearing rock near [[see:Johannesburg]]; its rand [[gave:rand]] the currency its name.
Delegation member possibly honoured by [[see:Johannesburg]]; a main street with a historic post office bears his name.
Delegation member sent to England for mining rights, possibly honoured by [[see:Johannesburg]]; a park is named after him.
Local administrator, another candidate for the Johan of [[see:Johannesburg]].
Stephanus Johannes Paulus Kruger, president of the South African Republic, another candidate for the name of [[see:Johannesburg]].
Zulu and Xhosa name for the [[see:Johannesburg]] area, meaning place of gold.
South African currency, named after the rand of [[from:Witwatersrand]].
Portuguese for lakes, after the Portuguese port city used for Atlantic exploration; earlier called [[see:Eko]] by the Yoruba-speaking Awori.
Awori name for the [[see:Lagos]] area, still a nickname for the city.
The hosts conclude it must be related to [[same-root?:lake]], prompted by the lagoon at Lagos.
Assumed by the hosts to be related to [[same-root?:lagoon]].
Named by the Fatimid dynasty; medieval writers wrongly linked it to [[see:Mars]]; the English form drops the article, maybe via Egyptian Arabic.
The vanquishing star, wrongly linked by medieval writers to the name [[see:Cairo]].
French name for [[see:Cairo]], keeping a definite article like the Arabic.
Village name meaning bag of salt, for the salt trade; renamed [[see:Leopoldville]] in 1881 and restored in 1966; may instead mean place of exchange.
Name given to [[see:Kinshasa]] in 1881 by [[see:Henry Morton Stanley]], after [[from:Leopold II]].
Welsh journalist who renamed Kinshasa [[see:Leopoldville]].
Belgian monarch after whom [[see:Leopoldville]] was named; the Belgians were reputedly particularly brutal colonialists.
Capital of Somalia, from Arabic [[from:Muqaddas]], holy, so holy place; [[gave:Madagascar]] was accidentally named after it.
Accidentally named after [[from:Mogadishu]], so it means the same.
Perhaps from Arabic khartum, elephant's trunk, for a strip of land between the Niles; more likely an Arabic twisting of a Dinka word, place where rivers meet.
Rob has talked about how it became Jorvik because people thought it meant place of the boar, though it didn't.
Looks like French bord, side, plus eau, waters, but an ancient name was adapted by [[see:folk etymology]] to match.
Matching sound and meaning, as with [[see:Bordeaux]]; addressed in another episode; also called [[see:folk etymology]].
Where a word's assumed origin influences its spelling, usage or definition; similar to [[see:phono-semantic matching]].
Rob recalls it comes from a cute variant of French Pierre, Peter, like [[see:parakeet]].
Also from a version of Pierre, like [[see:parrot]].
Named after the [[from:Parisii]]; Romans recorded it as [[from:Lutetia Parisiorum]], later shortened; like Berlin, it's named for a swamp.
Gallic tribe on the Seine who gave [[gave:Paris]] its name; their name may come from a root meaning cauldron, or mean makers, commanders or spear people.
Roman name for [[see:Paris]], recorded in Julius Caesar's writings in the 1st century BC.
Earlier name of [[see:Paris]], from a Celtic word meaning marsh or swamp.
Rob suggests their name may also mean spear people, like the [[see:Parisii]].
Often spelt with a final S in English but not French; a French adaptation of the Greek name [[from:Massalia]].
Means smoky bay, after the volcanic steam rising from the ground that struck the first settler.
Letter still used in conservative Icelandic that English once had, with [[see:eth]].
Letter still used in Icelandic that English once had, with [[see:thorn]].
Formerly [[from:Edo]], renamed in 1868 after the Meiji Restoration as the eastern capital, east of [[see:Kyoto]]; the shared kyo explains the anagram.
Original name of [[gave:Tokyo]], written with characters meaning river inlet and entrance; seat of the Tokugawa shogunate.
Means capital city, though no longer the capital; the emperors moved from it to Edo, renamed [[see:Tokyo]].
Jing means capital, so northern capital; [[see:Peking]] is an older English rendering, replaced via [[see:Pinyin]].
Means southern capital, the counterpart of [[see:Beijing]].
Older Anglophone rendering of the same Chinese name as [[see:Beijing]], surviving in the airport code PEK and in French.
Current romanization system for Mandarin, which gave the spelling [[see:Beijing]].
Means on top of the sea; hai means sea, so it marks coastal places.
Vast city named supposedly because an emperor was honoured there before his enthronement, giving a double celebration.
Pronounced with an ung sound; means becoming capital; it is the capital of [[see:Sichuan]] province, famous for pandas.
Province, as in Sichuan chicken; si means four and chuan rivers.
Means fragrant harbour, the fragrance probably from local agarwood trees.
Means broad island; its [[see:shima]] is the same element as the jima in [[see:Iwo Jima]].
Means sulfur island; renamed [[see:Iwo To]] in 2007; jima is [[see:shima]] changed by [[see:rendaku]].
Element meaning island, which becomes jima in compounds through [[see:rendaku]], and is written with the same character as to.
Japanese sound change in which an unvoiced consonant becomes voiced in a compound, turning [[see:shima]] into jima.
Name of [[see:Iwo Jima]] since 2007; still means sulfur island, written identically, only pronounced differently.
Means big or great hill; a traditionally mercantile, rougher-edged city than tidy [[see:Kyoto]], known for food.
Osaka dish, a pancake made with cabbage and topped with sauce, which Rob craves but struggles to find in Berlin.
